planting.note: Plant next to a trellis, fence, or pillar in spring or fall, angling canes at planting to encourage horizontal training and better bloom coverage; Compassion is a 1973 English climber especially valued for its strong, sweet fragrance.

directions: Plant next to a trellis, fence, or pillar in spring or fall, training and tying the flexible canes horizontally to maximize the number of flowering laterals. Compassion, a British climber introduced in 1973, bears high-centered, double flowers in a warm salmon-pink flushed with apricot, carrying one of the strongest fragrances of any modern climbing rose, a rich, fruity scent that has made it a long-standing favorite for arbors and walls near seating areas. It reblooms reliably through the season and shows good disease resistance for an older climber. Prune to shape and remove old, unproductive wood in late winter once the main framework of canes is established, leaving the horizontal side shoots that carry most of the flowers largely intact.

planting.note: Plant next to a trellis, fence, or pillar in spring or fall, angling canes to encourage horizontal training; Aloha is a vigorous but relatively short climber, well suited to a pillar or smaller structure.

directions: Plant next to a trellis, pillar, or fence in spring or fall, training the canes horizontally where possible to encourage more flowering side shoots. Aloha, introduced in 1949, bears large, fully double, cupped blooms in a rich coral-pink with a strong, sweet fragrance, on sturdy, relatively short climbing canes that make it a good choice for a pillar or smaller support rather than a large wall or arbor. Its thick, leathery, disease-resistant foliage and repeat-blooming habit through the season have kept it in steady cultivation for decades. Prune to remove old or unproductive wood in late winter once the framework of canes is established, and deadhead spent blooms through the season to encourage continued flowering.

common_name: Dublin Bay Rose (Bright Red Climbing Rose)

planting.note: Plant next to a trellis, fence, or pillar in spring or fall, angling canes to encourage horizontal training and heavier bloom; Dublin Bay is a compact, well-behaved climber good for smaller structures.

directions: Plant next to a trellis, pillar, or fence in spring or fall, training canes horizontally to maximize the number of flowering laterals. Dublin Bay, a New Zealand-bred climber introduced in 1975, bears clusters of bright, true-red, double blooms with light fragrance held above glossy, disease-resistant foliage, flowering nearly continuously from late spring through frost with better repeat bloom than many older climbers. Its moderate, well-mannered size makes it practical for a mailbox post, small arbor, or pillar rather than requiring a large wall. Prune out old or crowded wood in late winter, and deadhead spent blooms through the season to sustain the heavy repeat-flowering habit.

common_name: Altissimo Rose (Large Single Red Climbing Rose)

planting.note: Plant next to a trellis, fence, or pillar in spring or fall, training canes horizontally to encourage more flowering laterals; Altissimo is grown for its bold single flower form rather than a fully double bloom.

directions: Plant next to a trellis, pillar, or fence in spring or fall, angling canes for horizontal training. Altissimo, introduced in 1966, bears large, single, velvety deep-red flowers with prominent golden stamens, a bold, simple flower form that stands out among the many fully double climbers on the market and reads dramatically from a distance. It flowers repeatedly through the season, and the open form of each bloom makes the stamens easily accessible to pollinators. Its moderate size suits a pillar or fence, and it shows good disease resistance for an older climber. Prune out old or crowded wood in late winter, and deadhead spent blooms to encourage continued flowering through summer and fall.

common_name: Joseph's Coat Rose (Multicolor Yellow-Orange-Red Climbing Rose)

planting.note: Plant next to a trellis, fence, or pillar in spring or fall, training canes horizontally to encourage more flowering laterals; Joseph's Coat can be grown as a large shrub or trained as a moderate climber.

directions: Plant next to a trellis, pillar, or fence in spring or fall, or allow it to grow as a large freestanding shrub if no support is provided. Joseph's Coat, introduced in 1964 and named for the biblical coat of many colors, bears clustered double blooms that open yellow and orange and deepen to red as they age, so a single spray often shows several colors at once, all set against glossy, disease-resistant foliage. It reblooms through the season and can be trained as a moderate climber on a pillar or fence, or left unsupported as a large arching shrub. Prune to control size and shape in late winter, and deadhead spent clusters through the season to keep the colorful, repeat-flowering display going.

common_name: Handel Rose (Cream Edged in Pink Climbing Rose)

planting.note: Plant next to a trellis, fence, or pillar in spring or fall, training canes horizontally to encourage more flowering laterals; Handel is a distinctive bicolor climber best sited where its picotee edge can be seen up close.

directions: Plant next to a trellis, fence, or pillar in spring or fall, training canes horizontally to maximize flowering side shoots. Handel, introduced in 1965, bears distinctive double blooms in creamy ivory-white with a picotee edge of deep rose-pink along each petal margin, a striking bicolor pattern that sets it apart from most other climbers and is best appreciated up close, such as along an entryway or low arbor. It reblooms through the season with light fragrance, and its moderate height suits a fence or pillar rather than a very large wall. Prune out old or crowded wood in late winter once the main cane framework is established, and deadhead spent blooms to sustain repeat flowering through summer and fall.
